title: Matter and its properties
summary: Everything around you is matter. Learn the states, types and changes of matter.
cards.0.p: Anything that has mass and takes up space is called matter. Water, air, stone and you are all matter. Light, sound and heat are not matter. They carry energy or are energy themselves.
cards.0.key: Anything with mass and volume is matter.
cards.0.once.secenekler.0.neden: Light has no mass and takes up no space. Light only carries energy.
cards.0.once.secenekler.1.neden: Air is a mixture of gases and has mass and volume. A blown-up balloon shows this.
cards.0.once.secenekler.2.neden: Water vapor is water in the gas state, and it has mass and volume.
cards.1.p: In a solid, particles are packed tightly in order and vibrate in place. In a liquid, particles are close together but slide past each other. That is why a liquid takes the shape of its container. In a gas, particles are far apart and fast, and they fill the whole container.
cards.2.p: A substance that absorbs heat melts, evaporates, or goes straight from solid to gas, which is called sublimation. A substance that releases heat freezes, condenses, or goes straight from gas to solid, which is called deposition. In these changes the substance stays the same substance.
cards.3.p: An element is made of only one kind of atom (Fe, O₂) and cannot be broken into simpler substances. A compound forms when different atoms bond in a fixed ratio (H₂O), and it can be broken down by chemical means. Elements and compounds are both pure substances.
cards.3.key: O₂ is a molecule of an element, and H₂O is a molecule of a compound.
cards.4.p: In a mixture the substances keep their properties. A mixture that is the same everywhere, like sugar water, is homogeneous. One whose parts you can tell apart, like sandy water, is heterogeneous. Mixtures are separated by filtering or distillation.
cards.5.p: In a physical change the substance keeps its identity. In a chemical change a new substance forms. A change of color, gas given off, heat, light and a precipitate are clues of a chemical change. But boiling water also gives off gas.
cards.5.etk.soru: Put each event in the right group: does the substance keep its identity, or does a new substance form?
cards.5.etk.ogeler.0.2: It is a change of state. Both ice and water are H₂O.
cards.5.etk.ogeler.2.2: Sugar molecules spread through the water but do not change. When the water evaporates, the sugar is left behind.
cards.5.etk.ogeler.6.2: Iron turns into iron oxide with oxygen and moisture.
cards.5.etk.ogeler.8.2: Substances in the cut apple react with oxygen in the air.
cards.5.key: A physical change is often easy to reverse. A chemical change usually is not.
cards.6.p: Mass, volume and inertia belong to all matter, and they are called common properties. Density, melting and boiling point, and solubility are characteristic properties. You identify an unknown substance by these properties.
cards.6.key: 10 g of water and 100 g of water have the same density but different masses.
cards.6.once.soru: Two bottles have lost their labels, and both hold a colorless liquid. Which measurement tells you which one is water?
cards.6.once.secenekler.0.neden: Pure water boils at 100 °C at 1 atm. Boiling point is a characteristic property that identifies a substance.
cards.6.once.secenekler.1.neden: Every substance has mass, and it depends on the amount. So it does not identify the substance.
cards.6.once.secenekler.2.neden: Volume depends on the amount. Different liquids can have the same volume.
cards.7.p: Mass per unit volume is called density, and it is calculated with d = m / V. At the same temperature and pressure, every pure substance has a fixed density that identifies it. A substance less dense than water floats on it.
cards.7.etk.soru: d = m / V. Change the mass and volume: does the object float or sink in water? (Water: 1.00 g/cm³)
cards.7.etk.yorum.0.1: This substance is less dense than water and floats.
cards.7.etk.yorum.1.1: This substance has the same density as water and stays suspended in it.
cards.7.etk.yorum.2.1: This substance is denser than water and sinks.
cards.7.key: d = m / V  (water ≈ 1 g/cm³; ice ≈ 0.92 g/cm³. Iron ≈ 7.87 g/cm³)
cards.7.once.soru: Ice floats on water. How does the density of ice compare with water's?
cards.7.once.secenekler.0.neden: A substance less dense than water floats. Ice has a density of about 0.92 g/cm³, and water about 1 g/cm³.
cards.7.once.secenekler.1.neden: If it were denser than water, it would sink.
cards.7.once.secenekler.2.neden: If they were equal, it would stay suspended in the water.
cards.8.p:
• Matter is anything with mass and volume, and it has three states.
• An element does not break down, while a compound breaks into its elements by chemical means.
• Mixtures can be homogeneous or heterogeneous.
• In a physical change the identity stays the same. In a chemical change a new substance forms.
• Density, melting point and boiling point identify a substance.
quiz.0.q: Put each event in the right group.
quiz.0.e: In melting, sublimation, fogging (condensation) and dissolving, the substance stays the same. A burning candle gives CO₂ and water. In a cooking egg the proteins permanently lose their shape (denaturation) and link together. Tarnished silver forms silver sulfide.
quiz.1.q: Match each change of state with its name.
quiz.1.e: A solid melts when it turns into a liquid. A liquid freezes when it turns into a solid and evaporates when it turns into a gas. A solid turning straight into a gas is sublimation, and the reverse is deposition.
quiz.2.q: A substance has a mass of 54 g and a volume of 20 cm³. What is its density in g/cm³?
quiz.2.e: Density is mass per unit volume. d = m / V = 54 / 20 = 2.7 g/cm³. This is the density of aluminum.
quiz.3.e: H₂O forms from different atoms bonded in a fixed ratio, and electrolysis splits it into H₂ and O₂.
quiz.3.y.0: O₂ is a molecule with two atoms, but both atoms are oxygen. So it is a molecule of an element.
quiz.3.y.2: In salt water, salt and water mix without bonding to each other. It is a mixture whose ratio can vary.
quiz.3.y.3: Fe is made of one kind of atom and cannot be broken into simpler substances. So it is an element.
A:ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Heat water, watch the particles, mix substances and burn one.
A:adimlar.0.metin: The container holds water particles. Change the temperature and see how the particles are arranged. Then turn the water into a gas.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.tamam: In a gas the particles are far apart and fast, and they fill the whole container. In a solid they vibrate in place, and in a liquid they slide past each other. The particles are always the same water molecules. Only their arrangement and motion change.
A:adimlar.1.metin: You keep heating the ice and measure its temperature. The graph will show how the temperature changes over time.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.soru: While the ice melts, it keeps absorbing heat. What happens to its temperature?
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The heat absorbed goes into pulling the particles apart. So the temperature stays at 0 °C while melting and at 100 °C while boiling (at 1 atm). Mixtures, on the other hand, usually melt over a range of temperatures.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The ice absorbs heat, but its temperature does not rise while it melts. The heat goes into something else.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The ice is absorbing heat, not releasing it. So its temperature does not drop.
A:adimlar.2.metin: Look at the particles in the boxes. If different atoms are bonded in a fixed ratio, it is a compound. If substances sit together without bonding, it is a mixture.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: These molecules have two atoms, but both are oxygen. It contains only one kind of atom, so this substance is an element: O₂.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: In each molecule two hydrogens are bonded to one oxygen, so this substance is water (H₂O). Different atoms are bonded in a fixed ratio, so it is a compound.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Here H₂ and O₂ molecules sit together without bonding. So this is a mixture of two elements.
A:adimlar.3.metin: You will stir both glasses well. One has sugar and water, the other olive oil and water.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.soru: After stirring and waiting, which one is the same everywhere?
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Sugar dissolves in water and spreads evenly everywhere. Olive oil does not dissolve, and since it is less dense than water it rises to the top, forming two layers.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Oil and water do not mix. After waiting, the oil collects on top.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Stirring does not dissolve everything. After waiting, one of the glasses separates into layers.
A:adimlar.4.metin: What changes when ice melts? Watch the water molecules up close.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.soru: What happens to the water molecules when ice melts?
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Melting is a physical change. The molecule is still H₂O, and the substance is still water. Tearing paper and dissolving sugar are also physical changes.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.1.yazi: They split into H and O atoms
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Splitting water into its atoms takes a chemical method such as electrolysis. Melting does not do that.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Melted ice is still water. If you freeze it, it becomes ice again.
A:adimlar.5.metin: Now you are burning charcoal, which is carbon. The carbon atoms will meet oxygen molecules from the air.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Carbon and oxygen bond to form carbon dioxide (CO₂), and this is a chemical change. The atoms do not disappear. They bond in a new arrangement. Heat and light given off are also clues of a chemical change.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.1.yazi: It only turns into a gas
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: If only the state changed, the molecule would stay the same. Here carbon combines with oxygen to form a new substance.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Atoms do not disappear in a reaction. They only bond again with other atoms.
A:kapanis.0: Matter is anything with mass and volume. In a solid the particles are ordered and vibrate, in a liquid they slide past each other, and in a gas they are far apart and fast.
A:kapanis.1: A pure substance has a definite melting and boiling point. While the state is changing, the temperature stays constant. Pure water melts at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C at 1 atm.
A:kapanis.2: An element is made of one kind of atom, and a compound of different atoms bonded in a fixed ratio. In a mixture the substances do not bond to each other.
A:kapanis.3: A homogeneous mixture is the same everywhere, for example sugar water. In a heterogeneous mixture you can tell the parts apart, for example olive oil and water.
A:kapanis.4: In a physical change the substance stays the same, as in melting and dissolving. In a chemical change a new substance forms, as in burning and rusting.
